Canaanites
KAY-nun-ites
n. pl.
From Canaan, the son of Ham and grandson of Noah (Genesis 9:22, 10:6), whose descendants settled the land between the Jordan and the Great Sea. Webster 1828 has CANAANITE, a descendant of Canaan, an inhabitant of the land of Canaan. In Scripture the word carries at once a genealogy, a geography, and a verdict: the Canaanites are the people whose iniquity filled up the measure God had set, and whose land was given to Abraham’s seed by covenant grant.

Biblical Definition

The Canaanites are the settled inhabitants of the land promised to Abraham, named first in the table of nations and last in the Gospels. They head the standing list of the doomed peoples: the Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Girgashites, and the Jebusites (Genesis 15:21), and again in the sevenfold roll of Deuteronomy 7:1. The Lord did not hide His reason for the four-hundred-year delay: the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full (Genesis 15:16). Canaan was not seized from the innocent; it was taken from a civilization that had ripened in child sacrifice, temple prostitution, and the abominations catalogued in Leviticus 18. The conquest was a judicial act of the Judge of all the earth, executed through Israel as His instrument, and Israel was warned in the same breath that the same land would vomit her out for the same sins (Leviticus 18:28). Israel did not finish the work. The children of Israel dwelt among the Canaanites (Judges 3:5), and the leaven of that tolerated remnant runs through the whole book of Judges and out into the monarchy. Yet Scripture will not let the category harden into race. Rahab the Canaanite is in the genealogy of Christ, and a Canaanite mother in Matthew 15:22 gets from the Son of David what Israel’s own elders would not ask for.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines CANAANITE as a descendant of Canaan, the son of Ham, and an inhabitant of the land of Canaan; he notes the secondary use of the word for a trafficker or merchant, which follows the Hebrew idiom itself.

expand to see more

CANAANITE, n. — A descendant of Canaan, the son of Ham; an inhabitant of the land of Canaan, afterward called Palestine.

The Hebrew word came also to signify a merchant or trafficker, from the Canaanite’s trade along the coast — a sense the prophets use pointedly (Hosea 12:7; Zephaniah 1:11).

The plural denotes collectively the peoples dispossessed by Israel under Joshua, of whom seven nations are named in Deuteronomy 7:1.

Webster’s entry is purely descriptive, as the 1828 lexicon usually is with proper nouns; the moral weight of the word is supplied entirely by Scripture.

That the same root should mean both Canaanite and merchant is a small witness to how the ancient world knew these people: by their harbors and their trade, long before Israel knew them by their altars.

Key Scripture

Genesis 15:16 — "But in the fourth generation they shall come hither again: for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full."

Deuteronomy 7:1 — "When the LORD thy God shall bring thee into the land whither thou goest to possess it, and hath cast out many nations before thee, the Hittites, and the Girgashites, and the Amorites, and the Canaanites, and the Perizzites, and the Hivites, and the Jebusites, seven nations greater and mightier than thou;"

Judges 3:5 — "And the children of Israel dwelt among the Canaanites, Hittites, and Amorites, and Perizzites, and Hivites, and Jebusites:"

Joshua 24:11 — "And ye went over Jordan, and came unto Jericho: and the men of Jericho fought against you, the Amorites, and the Perizzites, and the Canaanites, and the Hittites, and the Girgashites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites; and I delivered them into your hand."

Matthew 15:22 — "And, behold, a woman of Canaan came out of the same coasts, and cried unto him, saying, Have mercy on me, O Lord, thou Son of David; my daughter is grievously vexed with a devil."

Modern Corruption

The conquest of the Canaanites is the standard modern charge against the God of the Old Testament — called genocide by the New Atheists and quietly disowned by progressive evangelicals who prefer a Jesus detached from the Judge of Genesis 15.

expand to see more

The charge that the conquest was genocide reads a judicial sentence as an ethnic policy. Genesis 15:16 settles the question of motive: the delay of four centuries was mercy, and the execution came only when the iniquity of the Amorites was full. Leviticus 18 names what filled it. The land is described as vomiting out its inhabitants, and the identical threat is pronounced over Israel herself in the same chapter — which is precisely what makes the conquest judicial rather than tribal. God did not favour Israel’s blood; He judged Canaan’s sin and warned Israel that her blood would not save her either. That warning was kept in 586 BC. A God who destroys Jericho and then exiles Jerusalem for the same offences is not a partisan deity.

The softer corruption is the Marcionite one that never announces itself: the practice of treating the Old Testament’s severity as a primitive layer that Jesus outgrew. Christ Himself said He came not to destroy the law and the prophets, and it is the Lamb of Revelation, not the Sinai lawgiver, who executes the final wrath. The proper answer to Canaan is not embarrassment but the Canaanite woman of Matthew 15:22, who received from Christ what her nation’s gods never gave, and Rahab, who is named in Hebrews 11 among the faithful. The line was never drawn by blood. It was drawn by faith, and it still is.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Kena’an (H3667) is both a personal name and a land; Kena’ani (H3669) is the gentilic, the Canaanite, and in a second sense the merchant.

expand to see more

Hebrew Kena’an (H3667) — Canaan; the son of Ham (Genesis 9:22) and the land named for him.

Hebrew Kena’ani (H3669) — Canaanite; used both of the people (Genesis 15:21) and, by trade, of a merchant (Hosea 12:7).

Greek Chananaios (G5478) — Canaanitish; used of the woman of Matthew 15:22 whom Mark calls a Syrophenician.

The sevenfold list of Deuteronomy 7:1 sometimes contracts to six or expands to ten (Genesis 15:19-21); the number is representative, not a census.

In many texts Canaanite stands for the whole population of the land, with the six other names as its subdivisions.

Usage

"The iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full (Genesis 15:16) — the four-hundred-year forbearance that precedes the conquest."

"Seven nations greater and mightier than thou (Deuteronomy 7:1) — the conquest is never presented as the strong overrunning the weak."

"A woman of Canaan came out of the same coasts (Matthew 15:22) — the doomed nation supplies one of the great confessions of faith in the Gospels."
